source.title: Internal Activation as the Polar Star for Steering Unsafe LLM Behavior
source.authors: Peixuan Han; Cheng Qian; Xiu-Si Chen; Yu-Ji Zhang; Denghui Zhang; Heng Ji

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes safety information in model hidden states, but does not test or rely on the claim that neuron poles have identifiable jobs, that neuron-based explanations generalize, or that neurons suffice as circuit units.
record.gate_note: The PCA visualizations and prober evaluations concern safety information in whole hidden states, not neuron poles or explanations of individual neurons. They are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. The paper's SafeSwitch benchmark results concern its safety method, not the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study probes whole hidden-state vectors for safety information and builds a safety-steering method (SafeSwitch). It never examines individual neurons, neuron poles, neuron explanations, simulation scoring, or neuron-based attribution graphs. It neither tests nor relies on any version of the claim. It mentions sparse autoencoders only in related work and does not cite the original sources, so 'discusses' overstates the link; 'cites_only' is the closest available relation.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that LLM internal states encode recognition of unsafe inputs and the intent to comply, and that two-stage probers predict unsafe outputs before generation. They also conclude that SafeSwitch, which activates a fine-tuned refusal head only when needed, cuts harmful outputs by about 80% while largely preserving utility and giving more informative refusals.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses PCA, SVMs, and trained MLP probers on whole hidden states, rather than neuron-pole explanations or tests of neuron explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Prober performance varies with layer depth and decoded-token count; the paper reports that deeper layers help and that decoding improves compliance prediction but harms unsafe-input detection.

fits_no_version.finding: PCA of residual-stream hidden states in four ~7-9B chat models shows safe/unsafe and complied/refused categories separating in deeper layers, with near-orthogonal SVM boundaries.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-related input classification and refusal decisions are linearly separable, near-orthogonal directions in deeper-layer hidden states.

fits_no_version.finding: MLP probers on whole hidden states predict unsafe responses; last-layer F1 is above 85%, and the two-stage prober with 3 decoded tokens exceeds 87% across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-state probers predict unsafe LLM behaviour before generation with high F1.

record.problems: The preliminary SVM accuracy is missing in the supplied text. Several layer- and token-specific prober results are presented in figures without exact values in the text. The paper notes prober errors and limitations, including false positives on XSTest and false negatives for some unsafe categories.

rows.subject: LLaMa-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Visualized hidden states across layers with 2D PCA and used SVM boundaries to separate safe/unsafe and complied/refused categories.

conditions.value: safe input; refused harmful input; complied harmful input

rows.measure: Qualitative separation of category representations in hidden states
rows.value: States are intermixed in early layers and become more distinct in later layers; deeper-layer boundaries are described as distinct and near-orthogonal.
rows.note: The paper states that the preliminary SVM method reaches less than an accuracy value, but the value is missing in the supplied text. This result concerns category information in whole hidden states, not individual neuron functions.

rows.subject: LLaMa-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Trained probers on internal states from different layers, using the last input token during prefilling.
rows.measure: F1 score for predicting unsafe behavior
rows.value: The last few layers yield F1 scores above 85%.
rows.note: The text does not provide exact values for the plotted layer-specific scores. This tests prediction from whole hidden states, not neuron explanations.

rows.subject: LLaMa-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared two-stage probers with direct probers on internal states.
rows.measure: F1 score difference between two-stage and direct probers
rows.value: Two-stage probers outperform direct probers by at least 4%.
rows.note: The paper reports the comparison qualitatively and does not give exact per-layer values in the text.
rows.check: Compares the study's own two-stage prober with its own direct-prober baseline, so this is a method comparison rather than a phenomenon finding.

rows.subject: LLaMa-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated probers after decoding different numbers of tokens.
rows.measure: Change in prober F1 with decoding
rows.value: Decoding a few tokens can improve compliance-prober performance while degrading unsafe-input-prober performance.
rows.note: The text gives no exact values for this comparison.
rows.check: State 'partial' is odd: the reported directional effect (compliance prober improves, unsafe-input prober degrades) is stated as observed. No exact values are given.

rows.subject: LLaMa-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated two-stage prober prediction using a prefill unsafe-input prober and a compliance prober after decoding three tokens.
rows.measure: F1 score for predicting unsafe behavior
rows.value: F1 scores over 87% across all models.
rows.note: This is an aggregate statement across models; the supplied text does not give model-specific values here.
rows.check: Subject should be all four base models (LLaMa-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Yi-1.5-9B, Ministral-8B), not LLaMa-3.1-8B alone; the F1>87% figure is stated across all models.
